extracted.intended_audience: historians and philosophers of science; graduate students and researchers in science studies
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and features for how scientific discoveries and new theories emerge, how crises arise in mature sciences, and what signals justify paradigm change or retooling. Useful for assessing the readiness, significance, and origins of purported scientific novelties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of discoveries that produce new kinds of phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Discoveries from which new sorts of phenomena emerge commonly display: prior awareness of anomaly; gradual and simultaneous emergence of observational and conceptual recognition; and consequent change of paradigm categories and procedures, often accompanied by resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three features (awareness of anomaly, concurrent observational/conceptual recognition, and paradigm change with resistance) are characteristic across examples; they indicate a discovery that genuinely creates a new sort of fact rather than merely filling in anticipated detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory-induced discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Speculative or unarticulated theories (not necessarily paradigm theories) can point the way to discovery; the actual discovery often differs from initial anticipation and emerges only when experiment and tentative theory are articulated to a match.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theory may direct experimental attempts even before it is mature; the discovery completes only when experimental results and conceptual interpretation cohere enough for the theory to function as a paradigm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal science prepares for novelty despite suppressing it
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal science, though not directed to novelties and tending initially to suppress them, is effective at producing the conditions for novelty because it constructs specialized apparatus, develops esoteric vocabulary/skills, and refines concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The professionalization and precision of normal science both narrow vision (resisting change) and provide the sensitive indicators (precise expectations and instruments) that reveal anomalies when something has gone wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of anomaly as prerequisite for theory change
rubrics_metrics.description: A profound awareness of anomaly — persistent failure of normal puzzles to resolve — is a prerequisite to acceptable changes of theory; prolonged and deep anomaly often produces a crisis that precedes major theory change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical cases show that novel theories arise after recognized failures; mere novelty or ad hoc problems do not usually motivate paradigm change unless anomalies penetrate core practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological/perceptual model of recognizing anomaly
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogous to perception experiments where anomalous stimuli are initially categorized as normal, scientists initially fit surprising results into existing categories and only with increased exposure or reflection do they experience hesitation, awareness, and conceptual adjustment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition of an anomaly typically proceeds from immediate misfit → hesitation/confusion → sudden conceptual adjustment for some observers; some never adjust. This explains the resistance and personal difficulty often accompanying discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proliferation of competing versions/theories as a symptom of crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: A crisis is often marked by many competing articulations or versions of a theory (proliferation of alternatives) as practitioners attempt to accommodate recalcitrant phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The multiplication of ad hoc variants signals that the reigning paradigm is losing its unique status and helps identify fields in crisis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breakdown of normal puzzle-solving activity indicates crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: When the normal technical problem-solving activity increasingly fails to produce expected results (complexity rising faster than accuracy, discrepancies recurring in different places), this technical breakdown is the core sign of a developing crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although external social factors can influence timing, the historical core of crises is the inability of established methods and rules to solve persistent technical problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: External factors modulate timing but do not substitute for technical breakdown
rubrics_metrics.description: Social pressures or external needs (e.g., calendar reform) can affect the timing, recognition, and locus of a crisis but do not replace the essential role of technical failure in producing a paradigm shift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claims of crisis by distinguishing external triggers from the deeper, technical failures in normal scientific practice that make theory replacement necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical temporal proximity of crisis and new theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Except in some special cases, the proliferation of theories and technical breakdown that constitute a crisis typically occur within a decade or two before the enunciation of a novel theory; the new theory appears as a fairly direct response to the immediately preceding crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the timing relation as evidence: long-standing but recently intensified anomalies that have produced theoretical proliferation are strong indicators that a new theoretical articulation may be imminent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipations of solutions are ignored without crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: Solutions or anticipations of a later successful theory are often proposed before the crisis but are typically ignored in the absence of recognized trouble; only when a crisis focuses attention are such anticipations taken seriously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical anticipations should not be taken as sufficient evidence that a field was ready for change; their neglect pre-crisis underscores the importance of perceived incompatibility with existing problem-solving practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneous independent emergence as an index of readiness
rubrics_metrics.description: When a significant scientific novelty emerges independently and nearly simultaneously in several laboratories, this is an index both of the traditional preparation by normal science and of the completeness with which that preparation readies the field for change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple independent occurrences strengthen the claim that the novelty reflects a real anomaly and a reliable basis for paradigm change rather than isolated error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance to change has a functional role
rubrics_metrics.description: Resistance within the scientific community to abandoning a paradigm helps ensure that paradigms are not too easily surrendered, preventing distraction by trivial anomalies and guaranteeing that only anomalies penetrating to the core prompt wholesale retooling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the quality of proposed changes in light of whether they overcome deep entrenched problems rather than responding to superficial discrepancies; resistance serves as a filter for robust revolution-worthy anomalies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-tooling is justified only when paradigm tools fail
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventing alternative theoretical constructions and retooling the discipline is an 'extravagance' reserved for occasions when the paradigm’s tools prove inadequate; crises signal the appropriate moment for such retooling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: prefer working within existing paradigm tools until persistent failures indicate necessity for constructing new tools and conceptual frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery and invention overlap; fact and theory are not categorically distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: In scientific practice, discovery (finding new phenomena) and invention (formulating new theory) overlap; the same historical episode may be described as discovery in one respect and invention in another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of novelties should attend to both empirical emergence and conceptual invention—recognizing that what counts as a 'discovery' can depend on the concurrent theoretical articulation.
